newsitem.title: INDIA: India-Pakistan talks go on despite Kashmir bombing.
newsitem.headline: India-Pakistan talks go on despite Kashmir bombing.

text.p: Indian and Pakistani diplomats went into a third day of talks on Sunday despite tension over a car bomb attack that police say killed 16 people and wounded about 70 in the northern city of Jammu.
Officials said Pakistan's foreign secretary Shamshad Ahmad and his Indian counterpart Salman Haidar met in New Delhi for the first of Sunday's two scheduled sessions.
The talks, exploring an agenda for an expected meeting of Indian and Pakistan foreign ministers next month, went ahead even though a senior official blamed Pakistan for the bombing.
Farooq Abdullah, chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir state, accused a Pakistani intelligence service of being behind Saturday night's blast at a crowded bus station.
"This dastardly act was sponsored by Pakistan's ISI (Inter-Services Intelligence) and its agents with the intention of dividing the people on communal lines," he said in a statement.
"The ISI doesn't want normalisation of relations between India and Pakistan and is...trying to create trouble in a bid to divide communities to further its ends," he added.
Jammu, winter capital of India's Moslem-majority state of Jammu and Kashmir, is populated mainly by Hindus.
No one has claimed responsibility for the attack and there has been no comment from Pakistan on Abdullah's allegation.
In further violence in Jammu and Kashmir, nine policemen were wounded on Sunday when an explosive device tied to the body of a slain guerrilla went off, police said.
The explosion occurred when police were examining the body in Kupwara police station near the India-Pakistan border 87 km (55 miles) north of Srinagar, the state's summer capital.
The India-Pakistan talks, reviving a dialogue that collapsed in January 1994 over Kashmir, have been shrouded in secrecy, with participants saying very little about their progress.

Pakistani spokesman Khalid Saleem said the two sides had discussed "all substantive issues" on Saturday, including the thorny issue of Kashmir, over which India and Pakistan have fought two of their three wars since independence in 1947.
Pakistan, which advocates a plebiscite in Kashmir to let its people choose whether to join India or Pakistan, wants "some progress" on the dispute before other issues can be tackled.

India says its sovereignty over Kashmir is not negotiable and has proposed putting the decades-old quarrel on the back burner. It would like agreements on promoting trade and economic cooperation and other confidence-building measures.
The Pakistani delegation is due to return home on Monday. The two countries' foreign ministers are expected to meet after an April 7-8 Non-Aligned Movement conference in New Delhi.
India accuses Pakistan of arming Moslem rebels fighting in the two thirds of Kashmir under Indian control.
Pakistan, which holds the rest of Kashmir, denies the charge, but says it supports the Kashmiris politicallly.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in Kashmir since the start of an armed revolt there in January 1990.
